feedback.nudge: The tail of a geometric distribution is a single power: $\P(X \ge n) = \rho^{\,n}$. Work out $\rho$ and raise it to the tenth.

explanation:
## The computation

$\rho = \lambda/\mu = 8/10 = 0.8 < 1$, so the chain is positive recurrent and the equilibrium distribution exists. Then

$$\P(X \ge 10) = \sum_{i \ge 10} (1-\rho)\rho^{\,i} = (1-\rho)\,\frac{\rho^{10}}{1-\rho} = \rho^{10} = 0.8^{10} \approx 0.1074,$$

so $\mathbf{0.107}$ to three decimal places.

The tail of a geometric distribution is a single power, which is the memorylessness of the geometric showing up: given that there are already ten customers, the number of *extra* ones has the same distribution as the whole queue length did.

## What else falls out of the same formula

| quantity | value here |
| --- | --- |
| server idle, $\pi_0 = 1-\rho$ | $0.2$ |
| mean number present, $\rho/(1-\rho)$ | $4$ |
| mean time in the system, $1/(\mu - \lambda)$ | $30$ minutes |
| mean queue length excluding the one in service | $\rho^2/(1-\rho) = 3.2$ |

The mean waiting time is Example 5.24(d) in the notes, and it comes out as $\E(\text{number present} + 1)/\mu$ by conditioning on the state an arriving customer finds.

## The shape of the answer, and why queues feel bad

$\rho/(1-\rho)$ is the number to keep in your head. It is not linear in the load:

| $\rho$ | $0.5$ | $0.8$ | $0.9$ | $0.95$ | $0.99$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| mean number present | $1$ | $4$ | $9$ | $19$ | $99$ |

Going from 50% to 80% utilisation quadruples the queue; going from 90% to 99% multiplies it by eleven. A server run at 99% of capacity is not "nearly perfectly used", it is a disaster waiting for a quiet period that never comes.

And the blow-up is entirely caused by **variability**. If arrivals came exactly every 7.5 minutes and each service took exactly 6 minutes, nobody would ever wait. It is the randomness of the Poisson arrivals and the exponential services that makes a queue form at all, which is why the Poisson process of chapter 4 has to come before this chapter.

## Where the geometric comes from

A birth–death chain is reversible, so instead of solving $\pi G = 0$ you can write down the balance across each edge of the chain:

$$\pi_i \lambda = \pi_{i+1}\mu \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \pi_{i+1} = \rho\,\pi_i \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \pi_i = \rho^i \pi_0,$$

and $\sum_i \pi_i = 1$ gives $\pi_0 = 1 - \rho$ provided the series converges, which needs $\rho < 1$.

The three regimes are worth naming. $\rho > 1$: transient, the queue runs away to infinity. $\rho = 1$: null recurrent — the queue keeps coming back to empty, and the expected time between empties is infinite. $\rho < 1$: positive recurrent, with the geometric equilibrium above.
